prompt.context: Our client is a small medical startup company that has invented a new ocular product which it believes will revolutionize the vision for people suffering from degenerative eye disease. The product has been patented however is yet to undergo clinical trials. The final product would need the patients to undergo a surgery and decrease the number of visits to the doctor. The first two stages of clinical trial is expected to cost our client $14M.
prompt.question: Our client is trying to decide if they should try and sell this technology to a major player, or should they raise capital and go to market with the product. What would you recommend?

clarifying_info.q: Are there any current buyers or acquirers interested in the technology?
clarifying_info.a: There are currently no buyers for this product, although some companies have expressed interest in investing in the technology for future rights.

framework: 1. Value proposition: differentiate the new ocular implant from current treatment and assess its value to patients
2. Clinical trial risk: recognize that trials may take years with no guarantee of success or FDA approval
3. Go-to-market feasibility: assess the capital required, infrastructure needs, and tort/liability implications of going to market independently
4. Partnership / funding options: evaluate obtaining investment from a major bio-med company to fund clinical trials in exchange for exclusivity or future rights
5. Insurance coverage: determine whether insurance will cover the device, affecting patient adoption and market size

questions.prompt: Compare the lifetime cost of the traditional treatment to the new ocular implant for an average patient.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate total cost of quarterly doctor visits over the disease lifetime vs. the one-time surgery plus annual fluid-check visits. Strong candidates will note the time-value of money (upfront lump sum vs. spread payments) and patient preference beyond pure cost.

math.setup: Disease onset age = 30; average life expectancy = 60; years of treatment = 30. Traditional: 4 visits/year at $350/visit. New implant: one-time surgery $37,250 + 1 annual visit at $75/visit.
steps: Traditional total = (60 - 30) years x 4 visits/year x $350/visit = 30 x 4 x 350 = $42,000
math.answer: Traditional method costs $42,000 lifetime; new implant costs $39,500 lifetime — a saving of $2,500. The saving is modest in absolute terms, but the implant offers additional patient benefits (clearer vision, fewer visits).

questions.prompt: Given the modest cost difference, what other factors should influence the client's decision?
questions.guidance: Candidate should address: (1) time value of money — lump-sum payment upfront is a larger immediate outlay even if lifetime cost is lower; (2) patient preference — research shows patients prefer the implant for quality-of-vision benefits even at higher cost; (3) market size — 9% of US population afflicted; (4) insurance reimbursement likelihood.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategic options should the client explore?

categories.name: Partnership / Funding
ideas: Approach major bio-med companies for investment to fund clinical trials in return for exclusivity rights
Seek venture capital or strategic investors who see long-term value in the patent
Explore government grants or NIH funding for clinical research

categories.name: Go-to-Market (Independent)
ideas: Raise capital and build internal commercial infrastructure
Partner with hospital networks for distribution
Hire experienced regulatory/FDA counsel to manage approval timeline

categories.name: Exit / IP Monetization
ideas: Sell or license the patent to a major player after clinical trials demonstrate efficacy
Auction exclusivity rights to multiple bidders to maximize sale price
Structure milestone-based payments tied to FDA approval

categories.name: Product Expansion
ideas: Investigate whether the implant platform can deliver other drugs
Explore treatment of other ocular or non-ocular diseases with the same device
Pursue international markets where regulatory pathways may be faster

recommendation: The client should approach major bio-med companies to secure investment for clinical trials in exchange for exclusivity, rather than attempting to go to market independently.
Post-trial, the client should consider selling or licensing the patent, given the significant infrastructure and capital requirements of commercialization.
risks: Clinical trials may take years and FDA approval is not guaranteed
No current buyers exist; negotiating leverage is limited until trial data is available
Going to market independently exposes the startup to substantial tort liability and capital risk
next_steps: Identify and approach 3-5 major bio-med companies with interest in ocular or implant technology
Quantify the market size (9% of US population) and prepare investor materials
Explore broader applications of the implant technology to enhance valuation
Assess insurance reimbursement landscape with a healthcare regulatory advisor
